extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students taking an introductory proofs course (and instructors designing such a course)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conventions for learning to prove theorems, focusing on elementary set theory, notation, and basic proof techniques; also guidance for instructors on course coverage and pacing. The material establishes precise definitions, notational conventions, and small-style rules that are prerequisites for writing clear, correct proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets are equal if they contain exactly the same elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality is determined by membership only (order and repetition do not matter). Examples: {2,4,6,8} = {4,2,8,6}; {2,4,6,8} ≠ {2,4,6,7}. Use this criterion when proving A = B: show each side's elements belong to the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for listing sets
rubrics_metrics.description: A set is often expressed by listing its elements between commas, enclosed by braces (e.g., {2,4,6,8}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uppercase letters commonly denote sets. Use membership notation x ∈ A and x ∉ A to state element facts. When sets are large or complex, prefer set‑builder notation: X = { expression : rule } read 'the set of all things of form expression such that rule.' Examples and alternatives (using a bar instead of a colon) are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set‑builder notation syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Set‑builder notation has the syntax X = { expression : rule }, where elements are all values of expression satisfying rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: E = {2n : n ∈ Z} for even integers; E = {n ∈ N : n is even}. The colon means 'such that'. Use this format for infinite or complicated sets; multiple equivalent descriptions are common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality (size) of a finite set
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a finite set, its cardinality |X| is the number of elements it has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation examples: |A| = 4 for A = {2,4,6,8}. Beware notation conflicts: |X| can mean absolute value when X is a number, so interpret from context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empty set vs singleton containing empty set
rubrics_metrics.description: The empty set ∅ is the set with no elements; do not confuse ∅ with {∅}, which is a set containing the empty set as an element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit caution: ∅ ≠ {∅} because ∅ has size 0 while {∅} has size 1. Use the box analogy (a set is a 'box' of things) to explain difference. This is a common error to avoid in proofs and notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of vertical bars (| · |)
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression |X| denotes absolute value when X is a number and cardinality when X is a set; the meaning should be clear from context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing proofs, ensure context makes clear which meaning of |·| is intended. Example contrasts: { x ∈ Z : |x| < 4 } (absolute value) vs B = { X ∈ A : |X| < 3 } (cardinality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Cartesian product and ordered pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cartesian product A × B is defined as A × B = { (a,b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B }, where (a,b) is an ordered pair and order matters: (2,4) ≠ (4,2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordered pairs to represent points and outcomes (e.g., product of dice rolls). Elements of A×B are ordered pairs; extend to n‑tuples for higher products. Visual diagrams (rows/columns) can help. When proving membership or equality involving products, use the definition: show first coordinate ∈ A and second ∈ B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality of Cartesian product (finite case)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are finite, then |A × B| = |A| · |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this fact to count outcomes (e.g., rolling a die twice gives 6·6=36 ordered pairs). Apply inductively for Cartesian powers A^n to compute |A^n| = |A|^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish product-parenthesization vs Cartesian power
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of parentheses: (R) × (N×Z) has elements of form (x,(y,z)), while R×N×Z consists of triples (x,y,z); these are formally different although often treated similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In proofs and definitions, keep parentheses explicit until it is safe to blur the distinction; recognize when objects are ordered pairs vs ordered triples vs sequences vs structured objects like matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subset definition and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: A is a subset of B (A ⊆ B) if every element of A is also an element of B. Write A ⊄ B when A is not a subset of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving A ⊆ B, show 'if x ∈ A then x ∈ B.' For A = B, prove mutual inclusion. Use counterexamples to demonstrate A ⊄ B. Remember universal truths like A ⊆ A and ∅ ⊆ B for any B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empty set is subset of every set
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact: The empty set ∅ is a subset of all sets (∅ ⊆ B for any set B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from the definition of subset because there is no element of ∅ that could fail membership in B. Use this fact in proofs about bases, vacuous truth, and constructions of subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting subsets (power set size)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a finite set B has n elements, then B has 2^n subsets (|P(B)| = 2^n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: use a binary 'insert or not' tree (or correspondence with binary strings) to list/count subsets. This is a standard combinatorial technique used in proofs and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention: elements of sets can be of any type (including sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of a set can be numbers, points, functions, matrices, or even other sets; treat them according to their type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate nested sets and how membership differs from elementhood of inner sets; be explicit when writing proofs that involve sets-of-sets to avoid confusion (e.g., specifying whether '2 ∈ E' vs '{2} ∈ E').

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and style cautions for proof clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful and explicit with notation (braces, parentheses, bars, ordered pairs) to avoid ambiguity that can invalidate an argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific cautions in the text: do not write {∅} when you mean ∅; resolve |·| ambiguity by context; keep parentheses to distinguish (x,(y,z)) from (x,y,z); clarify when a set is being treated as a sequence or matrix. These small notation choices matter in formal proofs and should be made deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course coverage guidance for instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is designed for a three- or four-credit course; instructors may omit certain chapters or sections depending on course emphasis (e.g., omit Chapter 3 Counting or Chapter 13 Calculus proofs). Sections marked with an asterisk may require only brief mention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested semester timetable is provided (14-week outline). Use the provided dependency tree to choose material consistent with students' backgrounds and course goals; the author indicates which chapters form the core and which can be left out without breaking continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning objective: transition from computational to theoretical mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary pedagogical aim: to initiate students into the theoretical realm where the goal is to understand mathematical structures and prove statements (not merely compute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should learn the methods mathematicians use to verify theorems, write proofs, and think critically. Course organization is designed to build language (sets, logic) first, then proof techniques (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction), and finally applications (relations, functions, cardinality). Use this objective to evaluate whether student proofs demonstrate understanding rather than only perform computations.
